method: Headlines from the source feed, read by Claude: summary and four beats in Blue Street's own words from each article's headline and public text; impact = which way the headline pushes each market (dir bullish/bearish/mixed, strength 1 mild, 2 clear, 3 strong). Evidence, not a call.

USD.text: The dollar is at its highest since April 2025 because Federal Reserve officials, including New York's John Williams, say inflation is too high and rates must keep rising. The costs are showing: US home sales are at their slowest since 2010, and the government's record October deficit means more bond sales on top.

EUR.text: The euro has fallen to about $1.11, its lowest since May 2025, as hot US inflation and talk of more Federal Reserve rate rises lift the dollar. Economists expect the European Central Bank to raise rates in December, but most think that will be its last rise, which offers the euro less support than the Fed's longer path.

GBP.text: Britain's economy grew 0.7% in the third quarter, in line with forecasts, which backs last week's Bank of England rise to 4% and leaves another in December likely. The pound is firm against the euro but held back against a dollar boosted by US rate talk.

JPY.text: The dollar briefly rose above 160 yen on Thursday night, a level where Japan and the US stepped in to buy yen in September, because US rates are far above Japan's. Japanese officials keep warning about the fast fall and a December Bank of Japan rise is expected, but neither has stopped the slide so far.

CHF.text: The Swiss franc slipped to a two-week low on Wednesday as the dollar climbed on bets of bigger Federal Reserve rate rises. Attacks on ships near the Strait of Hormuz keep some safe-haven demand alive, but for now higher US rates matter more.

CAD.text: Oil, Canada's main export, is back near $96 after attacks on Saudi oil sites and tankers near Hormuz, and the Bank of Canada says it is ready to raise rates again if energy costs spread. But Canada has lost jobs two months running and the loonie sits near a 19-month low against a strong US dollar.

AUD.text: The Australian dollar is weighed down by a strong US dollar and by falling tech shares after Nvidia's chief executive quit. At home, new home loans and consumer confidence have dropped, signs the 4.85% cash rate is biting that make another Reserve Bank of Australia rise less likely.

NZD.text: The New Zealand dollar led the major currencies on Monday, up about 1.5% to near 56 US cents, as calmer markets and Saturday's election, which left Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's three-party bloc just ahead, gave it some relief. About 400,000 votes are still to count, so who governs may not be clear until November 27, and the jobless rate is already at its highest since 2015. Stronger-than-expected Chinese imports in October are a small extra help.

XAU.text: Gold has dropped below $3,900 an ounce, its lowest in over a year, as Federal Reserve officials promise more rate rises and 10-year US bond yields sit above 5%. That outweighs demand from the Middle East war for now.

OIL.text: Oil jumped back toward $96 a barrel on Thursday after Yemen's Houthis said they hit Saudi oil sites, including the pipeline Saudi Arabia uses to bypass Hormuz, and Iran claimed tanker hits in the strait. Rising US stockpiles and higher OPEC+ output still cap the gains.

items.headline: Fed's Williams says inflation stubbornly high and Fed still has work to do on policy
items.story_title: Fed: how fast to raise rates after hot inflation
items.summary: New York Fed President John Williams said inflation is too high and slow to fall, and the Federal Reserve will need to keep acting over time to bring it back to 2%.

beats.was: US consumer prices rose faster than expected in October, and several Federal Reserve officials have since backed more rate rises. Markets treat a quarter-point rise at the December 9 meeting as close to certain.
beats.happened: Speaking at an event in New York on Thursday evening, Williams called the economy strong and growing but not overheating, and said rates are not yet where they need to be. He did not commit to a size for December.
beats.means: Williams is the Fed's vice chair on rate decisions and usually speaks for its leadership, so his view backs the December rise and more after it. By not pushing a half-point step, he leaves the pace about where markets had it.
beats.fx: Keeps US rates heading higher than most others, which supports the dollar and weighs on gold, which pays no interest.

impact.why: The Fed's number two backs further rate rises, in line with what markets expect.
Higher expected US rates make holding gold less attractive.

items.watch: US producer prices and retail sales, and whether any senior official starts arguing for a half-point rise.

items.headline: Asia FX: yen intervention in focus as rate hike bets put dollar near 19-mth high
items.story_title: Japan's fight to prop up the yen
items.summary: The US dollar briefly rose above 160 Japanese yen overnight before settling just under it in Asian trading on Friday, a level where Japan has stepped in before.

beats.was: US interest rates are far above Japan's, which has pushed the yen down for months. In September, Japan and the US acted together to buy yen, and Japanese officials have warned again this week as the yen slid back toward 160 per dollar.
beats.happened: The dollar crossed 160 yen for a short time on Thursday night, then traded near 159.96 on Friday. Japanese officials again warned against one-sided currency moves, and top currency official Atsushi Mimura said it was too early to forget the September action.
beats.means: The line Japan has defended before has now been touched, so the chance of Japan buying yen again is rising. Until it does, the gap in rates keeps pulling the yen lower.
beats.fx: Steady pressure on the yen from US rates, with a risk of a sudden yen jump if Japan steps in.

impact.why: The yen touched 160 per dollar as the rate gap with the US keeps widening.
The dollar is set for a third weekly rise on bets of more Federal Reserve rate rises.

items.watch: Whether Japan buys yen if the dollar stays above 160, Japan's third-quarter growth and October inflation figures next week, and US producer prices on Friday.

items.headline: US starts 2027 fiscal year with record October budget deficit of $404 billion
items.story_title: US government borrowing keeps growing
items.summary: The US government spent $404 billion more than it took in during October, the most ever for that month, as tax and tariff income fell and spending hit a record.

beats.was: The US ran a deficit of nearly $2 trillion in the year to September, about 6.2% of the economy and the biggest in five years. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent wants to cut it to 3%.
beats.happened: The Treasury said the October gap was 42% bigger than a year earlier. Income fell 9%, with tariff collections down 39% from their peak, while spending rose 12% to a record on farm aid, military payments and higher interest on the debt.
beats.means: A bigger gap means the government must sell more bonds, which adds upward pressure on US borrowing costs, already above 5% for 10-year bonds. Interest on the debt is itself one of the fastest-rising costs.
beats.fx: Higher bond yields help the dollar for now, but steady talk of big deficits is also one of the reasons some buyers prefer gold over US assets.

impact.why: More bond sales lift yields, which helps the dollar, but a growing debt load is a long-run worry.
Higher yields weigh on gold, while deficit worries support it over time.

items.watch: Demand at upcoming US bond auctions and whether tariff income keeps falling.

items.headline: Gold, silver slide as Treasury yields surge, Fed hike concerns intensify
items.story_title: Gold: rising US rates vs war risk
items.summary: Gold fell almost 3% on Thursday to about $3,876 an ounce, below $3,900, as US government bond yields jumped on bets the Federal Reserve will keep raising rates.

beats.was: US consumer prices rose faster than expected in October, and Federal Reserve officials have since talked up more rate rises. Gold had already slipped below $4,000 on Wednesday.
beats.happened: Spot gold dropped about $110 and silver fell about 3% to near $50. The 10-year US Treasury yield rose to about 5.10%, and futures put the chance of a December Fed rise at near certain, with about a one-in-seven chance of a bigger half-point move.
beats.means: Gold pays no interest, so when safe US bonds pay over 5% it loses appeal, and a strong dollar makes it dearer for buyers abroad. For now that outweighs the pull from the Middle East war.
beats.fx: Higher US yields back the dollar; the fall in gold and silver is a mild drag on Australia's metal-heavy exports.

impact.why: Higher US yields and a firm dollar cut gold's appeal.
Rising Treasury yields reflect bets on more Fed rate rises.
Cheaper metals trim Australia's export income.

items.watch: US producer prices next, Fed speakers' views on a half-point move, and whether war news brings back safe-haven buying.

items.headline: Oil settles $3 higher on attacks on Saudi energy sites, Strait of Hormuz disruptions
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: Oil jumped more than 3% on Thursday after Yemen's Houthi group said it attacked Saudi oil sites, on top of Iranian claims of tankers hit in the Strait of Hormuz. Brent closed near $96 a barrel.

beats.was: Since the US and Israel went to war with Iran in late February, the Strait of Hormuz, the route for about a fifth of the world's oil, has been restricted. Saudi Arabia's pipeline to the Red Sea port of Yanbu is its main way to ship oil around the strait.
beats.happened: The Houthis, an Iran-backed group in Yemen, said they struck a pumping station on that Saudi pipeline, an oil site at Yanbu and a Saudi Aramco building in Riyadh. The Saudi-led coalition said it shot down two drones. Brent settled at $95.82, up $3.06, and US crude at $88.74, though both are still down about 2.5% on the week.
beats.means: The war's risks are no longer just inside the strait: the route Saudi Arabia uses to get around it is now a target too. That makes it harder for supply to recover even if ship traffic through Hormuz picks up.
beats.fx: Dearer oil helps the Canadian dollar and hurts big oil importers such as Japan and the euro area.

impact.why: Attacks on Saudi Arabia's bypass pipeline threaten the main way around Hormuz.
Higher oil prices help Canada's biggest export.
Japan buys almost all its oil abroad, so its import bill rises.
The euro area imports most of its energy.

items.watch: Whether Saudi Arabia confirms any damage or lost flows, more Houthi attacks, and the International Energy Agency's monthly oil report on Friday.

items.headline: Fed's Goolsbee Says Inflation 'Inching' Into Tough Spot
items.story_title: Fed: how fast to raise rates after hot inflation
items.summary: Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee said the Federal Reserve has to act on inflation before the economy overheats, adding to the run of officials backing more rate rises.

beats.was: US consumer prices rose more than expected in October, and markets now treat a December Fed rate rise as close to certain. The open question is how fast and how far rates go after that.
beats.happened: Speaking on Yahoo Finance, Goolsbee said inflation is moving into a difficult place and the Fed should move before price pressures build further. He did not call for a bigger half-point step.
beats.means: Goolsbee is usually one of the more cautious officials, so his support for acting firms up the December rise and the case for more after it.
beats.fx: Supports the dollar against currencies whose central banks are closer to stopping.

impact.why: A usually cautious Fed official backs further rate rises.

items.watch: New York Fed President John Williams' remarks, US producer prices, and any official openly calling for a half-point rise.

items.headline: Iran says four tankers were hit by explosions in the Strait of Hormuz
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: Iran's military says four oil tankers were hit by explosions in the Strait of Hormuz over Wednesday and Thursday after ignoring its warnings. Reuters could not check the claim, but oil rose to a new high for the day.

beats.was: The US and Israel went to war with Iran in late February, and Iran has since restricted the Strait of Hormuz, the route for about a fifth of the world's oil. Ship traffic had been recovering on hopes of a US–Iran deal.
beats.happened: Iran's Revolutionary Guards said two large tankers blew up on Wednesday after taking a route it had not approved, and its army said two more hit mines and caught fire on Thursday. A UK shipping agency separately reported a ship struck by a projectile off the United Arab Emirates on Wednesday. At least 10 ships have been hit so far this month, after 37 in October.
beats.means: Even with traffic picking up, Iran is showing it can still stop tankers at will, and this comes the same day President Trump said the US no longer needs a deal. Brent rose above $95 a barrel.
beats.fx: Higher oil and more war risk help the Canadian dollar and weigh on big oil buyers such as Japan and the euro area.

impact.why: Fresh attacks on tankers in the main Gulf oil route keep supply at risk.
Dearer oil helps Canada's main export.
Japan imports nearly all its oil, so a higher bill hurts.
The euro area is a big energy importer.

items.watch: Whether shipping firms pause Hormuz trips again, any independent confirmation of the hits, and the International Energy Agency's monthly oil report on Friday.

items.headline: Stock market today: S&P 500, Nasdaq sink as Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns, stock tanks
items.story_title: Nvidia: chief executive Jensen Huang steps down
items.summary: Jensen Huang, Nvidia's co-founder and chief executive, resigned with immediate effect on Thursday; the shares fell 7–10% in early New York trading and pulled the Nasdaq lower.

beats.was: Nvidia, the chipmaker at the centre of the AI boom and one of the world's biggest companies, has been under pressure since newspaper reports about Huang's personal conduct led its board to open an investigation last weekend. On Wednesday night the board met to decide his future.
beats.happened: Nvidia said Huang has left as chief executive, president and board member, effective at once. Finance chief Colette Kress takes over for now until a permanent pick is named. Nvidia shares dropped sharply at the New York open, other chipmakers slipped, and the Nasdaq fell close to 1% while the wider S&P 500 lost less.
beats.means: The man most linked to the AI rally is gone, which hits confidence in the tech shares that have led global stocks. So far the selling is mostly inside tech, not a broad flight from risk, and currency moves are small.
beats.fx: A small pull toward safe havens such as the yen and Swiss franc and away from risk-linked currencies like the Australian dollar, which would grow only if the selling spreads to the wider market.

impact.why: A tech-led stock drop can draw some safe-haven buying.
Weaker stocks weigh on currencies tied to risk appetite.
Mild safe-haven pull if the selling widens.

items.watch: Whether the stock slide spreads beyond chipmakers through the US session, and who Nvidia names as its permanent chief executive.

items.headline: Brent Rises to $93.29 as Trump's No-Deal Iran Remarks Revive War Premium
items.story_title: US–Iran talks: Hormuz reopening offer vs ship attacks
items.summary: US President Donald Trump said on Thursday the US does not need a deal with Iran and claimed control of the Strait of Hormuz, nudging Brent crude back up to about $93 a barrel.

beats.was: Since the US–Iran war began, ships near the Strait of Hormuz, the route for about a fifth of the world's oil, have been attacked again and again. Oil had dropped earlier this week on hopes of direct US–Iran talks, and US crude is down about 16% in November.
beats.happened: Trump said a deal with Iran is not needed and that the US has control of the strait. Brent rose about 0.5% to $93.29 while US crude was little changed near $86, undoing part of the earlier drop.
beats.means: The remarks cast doubt on a quick peace deal, so some of the war risk that had been taken out of oil prices is coming back. Analysts also warn the claim of US control could invite more attacks on ships.
beats.fx: Firmer oil gives a little help to the Canadian dollar and weighs a little on oil importers such as Japan and the euro area.

impact.why: Doubt over a deal puts some war risk back into the price.
Canada's main export gets a small lift.
Japan imports nearly all its oil, so dearer crude is a small drag.

items.watch: Whether Tehran responds to Trump's claim, any new attacks on ships near Hormuz, and whether the reported meeting between US Vice President JD Vance and Iran's security chief Mohsen Rezaei goes ahead.

items.headline: US weekly jobless claims increase, but labor market firming
items.story_title: US jobs: hiring holds up as the Fed raises rates
items.summary: New US claims for unemployment benefits rose to 200,000 last week, a little more than the 195,000 forecast but still very low, so the job market still looks firm.

beats.was: The US job market has been strong: employers added many more jobs than expected in October and the jobless rate fell to 4.1%. With inflation back up, the Federal Reserve is expected to raise rates in December, and a solid job market supports that.
beats.happened: First-time claims for jobless benefits, a weekly read on layoffs, rose by 9,000 to 200,000 in the week to November 7, slightly above forecasts. The number of people still claiming benefits fell by 20,000 to about 1.7 million. Claims have stayed at or under 200,000 since mid-September, close to their lowest since 1969.
beats.means: Layoffs remain rare, so nothing here argues against a December Fed rate rise. The small miss is noise; it would take a clear jump in claims to change the Fed's path.
beats.fx: Little change for the dollar; it keeps the backing of a firm job market and a Fed still raising rates.

impact.why: Claims a touch above forecast, but still low enough to keep the Fed on course to raise rates.

items.watch: Federal Reserve speakers later this week, and next month's US jobs report before the December Fed meeting.

items.headline: US existing home sales slump to more than 16-year low in October
items.story_title: US housing: high mortgage rates choke sales
items.summary: Sales of previously owned US homes fell 5.5% in October to the slowest pace since August 2010, as 30-year mortgage rates stay above 7%.

beats.was: The Federal Reserve has been raising rates to fight inflation, and 30-year mortgage rates are near their highest since 2000.
beats.happened: The National Association of Realtors said sales fell to a yearly pace of 3.75 million, below the 3.85 million economists expected and 8.8% lower than a year ago. Prices still rose slightly, to a median of about $422,000, because few homes are for sale.
beats.means: Higher rates are clearly hurting the housing market, one of the first parts of the economy to feel them. It is a sign of strain but not yet enough to change the Fed's plan to raise rates in December.
beats.fx: A mild drag on the dollar's growth story, outweighed for now by hot inflation and Fed rate-rise bets.

impact.why: Weak home sales show high rates are slowing part of the economy.

items.watch: Whether weakness spreads to building and spending data, and if Fed officials start to mention it.

items.headline: Dollar reaches 19-month high as rate expectations dominate
items.story_title: Fed: how fast to raise rates after hot inflation
items.summary: The dollar rose to its highest since April 2025 on Thursday, pushing the euro down to about $1.106 and the yen to almost 160 per dollar, as traders bet on more Federal Reserve rate rises.

beats.was: Hotter-than-expected US inflation this week led Fed officials and big banks to call for further rate rises, while other central banks are closer to stopping.
beats.happened: The dollar index, which tracks the dollar against six major currencies, rose 0.3% to about 103.2. Futures put a December Fed rise at about 91%, and Goldman Sachs expects another early next year. The 10-year US yield sat near 5.07%.
beats.means: The dollar's climb rests almost entirely on the gap between US rates and everyone else's, so it now depends on Fed officials keeping that path alive.
beats.fx: Broad pressure on the euro and the yen, with Japan's warnings about a weak yen growing louder near 160.

impact.why: Bets on more Fed rate rises keep lifting the dollar.
The euro fell to its lowest since spring 2025 as the rate gap widens.
The yen nears 160, where Japan has warned it may step in.

items.watch: US producer prices, Fed speakers, and any sign Japan steps in to buy yen.

items.headline: Trump Takes Vance Off Iran Talks, Says US Doesn't Need a Deal
items.story_title: US–Iran talks: Hormuz reopening offer vs ship attacks
items.summary: US President Donald Trump told Vice President JD Vance to drop his work on Iran talks and focus on fraud at home, saying a deal with Iran is no longer needed. Oil rose on the news.

beats.was: The US and Israel went to war with Iran in late February, and Iran has since choked off the Strait of Hormuz, the route for about a fifth of the world's oil. On Wednesday, reports said Vance was weighing a rare face-to-face meeting with a senior Iranian security official.
beats.happened: On Thursday Trump wrote on social media that Vance should give his full attention to fraud in the US instead, and that the time for a deal with Iran has passed because the US already holds Iran's money and the strait.
beats.means: The most direct channel for peace talks has been shut for now, so hopes of a quick end to the war, which had pulled oil lower this week, have faded.
beats.fx: Less chance of a deal keeps oil supported, a small help for the Canadian dollar and a small drag on big oil importers such as Japan and the euro area.

impact.why: A quick peace deal looks less likely, so war risk stays in the price.
Firmer oil helps Canada's main export.
Japan buys nearly all its oil abroad.

items.watch: Any reply from Tehran, whether US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner pick up the Iran file, and new attacks on ships near Hormuz.

items.headline: Fed's Daly says more rate rises are likely, but there's no rush
items.story_title: Fed: how fast to raise rates after hot inflation
items.summary: San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly said the Federal Reserve will probably need to raise rates further, though higher bond yields give it time to move carefully.

beats.was: US consumer prices rose faster than expected in October, and several Federal Reserve officials have since backed a rate rise in December, with some talking about more after that.
beats.happened: Speaking at Stanford on Thursday, Daly said her bias is that more tightening will be needed, because price rises are spreading from energy and goods into services, where they tend to stick. She said AI is only a small part of the inflation problem and that rising bond yields buy the Fed time.
beats.means: Another Fed official, usually seen as middle-of-the-road, now leans toward more rises, but her 'no rush' tone points to steady steps rather than a bigger jump.
beats.fx: It backs the case for higher US rates that has lifted the dollar, adding little that markets had not already expected.

impact.why: One more Fed voice backing further rate rises.
Higher US rates make gold, which pays no interest, less attractive.

items.watch: US retail sales and producer prices for October, and whether more Fed officials talk about a half-point move.

items.headline: US Crude Stocks Rise 4.66 Million Barrels Against an Expected Drop
items.story_title: US oil stockpiles
items.summary: Official US data showed crude stockpiles rose by about 4.7 million barrels last week when a small drop was expected, with fuel stocks also building.

beats.was: Each week the US Energy Information Administration (EIA) reports how much crude and fuel sits in US storage. A private survey from the American Petroleum Institute on Tuesday had already pointed to a large crude build of 9 million barrels.
beats.happened: The EIA said crude stocks rose 4.66 million barrels in the week to November 6, against forecasts of a 1.1 million drop. Gasoline rose 1.8 million barrels and diesel and heating oil 4.1 million, both against expected small falls.
beats.means: More oil in storage points to softer US demand or ample supply, a mild weight on prices. But the build was smaller than the private survey suggested, and the Iran war matters far more for oil right now.
beats.fx: Little direct effect on currencies; any lasting dip in oil would be a small minus for the Canadian dollar.

impact.why: Bigger stockpiles than expected point to ample supply.
Softer oil is a small drag on Canada's main export.

items.watch: The International Energy Agency's monthly oil report on Friday and next week's EIA figures on Wednesday, November 18.

items.headline: Fed's Hammack signals support for gradual rate-hike path
items.story_title: Fed: how fast to raise rates after hot inflation
items.summary: Beth Hammack, president of the Cleveland Federal Reserve, said on Thursday the Fed should keep raising rates in small, steady steps rather than switch to bigger moves.

beats.was: The Federal Reserve raised its rate to 3.75%–4.00% in September, then held in October while Hammack voted for a rise. After October's US inflation came in hotter than expected, Governor Christopher Waller said a half-point rise in December should be considered.
beats.happened: Hammack said inflation is heading the wrong way but the Fed is not yet behind the curve. She argued that steady, smaller and more frequent rises are less disruptive than larger ones.
beats.means: A hawkish official is backing more rises, but at the usual quarter-point pace. That supports a December rise while cooling talk of a jump to half a point.
beats.fx: Keeps support under the dollar from a longer run of rate rises, but trims the extra lift that a bigger December move would bring.

impact.why: More rises backed, but in quarter-point steps rather than a half-point jump.
Higher US rates weigh on gold, but less talk of a bigger move eases the pressure a little.

items.watch: Comments from New York Fed President John Williams later Thursday, and whether other officials side with steady quarter-point rises or with Waller's half-point option for the December 8–9 meeting.

items.headline: Dovish BOJ policymaker Asada pushes back against early rate hike
items.story_title: BoJ: a rate rise in December?
items.summary: Toichiro Asada, a Bank of Japan board member who voted against the last two rate rises, warned that raising rates too soon could hurt growth and push inflation back down.

beats.was: The Bank of Japan has been lifting its rate step by step and markets expect another rise at its December 17–18 meeting, while the yen trades near 160 per dollar. Asada is the board's best-known opponent of faster rises and voted against the moves in June and September.
beats.happened: In a speech in Nagasaki on Thursday, Asada said past and future rate rises could weigh on activity and on underlying inflation, and that the pace of any further rises should be weighed carefully. He welcomed wages beating inflation this year but said spending and growth lack momentum.
beats.means: It is one dissenting voice, and markets still see a December rise as likely. But it reminds traders the board is split, which caps how fast Japan's rates can rise.
beats.fx: A small weight on the yen, which is already near 160 per dollar, the level where Japan bought yen this summer.

impact.why: A known dove's caution, not a shift by the board majority.

items.watch: Comments from Governor Kazuo Ueda or his deputies before December, and whether Japan steps in to buy yen if it breaks 160.

items.headline: Japan wholesale inflation accelerates, keeps alive BOJ rate-hike view
items.story_title: BoJ: a rate rise in December?
items.summary: Prices that Japanese companies pay each other rose 7.1% in the year to October, faster than the 6.5% expected, partly because the weak yen makes imports dearer.

beats.was: The Bank of Japan has been slowly lifting its rate from near zero and now sits at 1.25%. Markets expect another rise at its December 17–18 meeting, while the yen trades close to 160 per dollar, a level where Japan stepped in to buy yen this summer.
beats.happened: Japan's wholesale price index, which tracks what firms pay for goods, rose 7.1% from a year earlier in October, up from 6.8% in September and above forecasts of 6.5%. Import prices measured in yen jumped about 25%, showing the cheap yen is pushing up the cost of raw materials.
beats.means: Rising costs for companies tend to reach shop prices later, which gives the Bank of Japan more reason to raise rates in December. It also shows the weak yen is now a source of inflation, which makes officials less willing to let it fall further.
beats.fx: Supports the yen by firming the case for a December Bank of Japan rise, though the pull of much higher US rates still weighs on it for now.

impact.why: A clear beat that strengthens the case for a Bank of Japan rate rise in December.

items.watch: Japan's October consumer prices later this month and any hint from Bank of Japan officials on December; a quiet reaction from them would leave the yen at the mercy of US rates.

items.headline: Japan warns again as yen nears 160 per U.S. dollar
items.story_title: Japan's fight to prop up the yen
items.summary: Japan's top currency official warned again that the yen is falling too fast, as the dollar reached 159.94 yen on Thursday morning, its highest in over two months.

beats.was: Japan spent record sums buying yen in late July and early August, once reportedly together with the US, after the dollar rose above 160 yen. Hot US inflation figures this week have pushed the dollar back toward that level.
beats.happened: Atsushi Mimura, Japan's vice finance minister for international affairs, said recent moves were too rapid and that it is too early to forget what happened this summer, without commenting on any exact rate. The dollar touched 159.94 yen in Tokyo trading.
beats.means: Tokyo is reminding traders that it has stepped in near 160 before and could again. Words alone rarely turn the yen for long while the gap between US and Japanese interest rates stays this wide.
beats.fx: Wider rate gaps push the yen weaker; the rising chance of official yen buying pushes the other way.

impact.why: A repeat warning from Tokyo near the level where it bought yen this summer.
The dollar's climb against the yen meets resistance from Japanese officials.

items.watch: Firmer language such as a 'final warning', sudden sharp yen gains that hint at official buying, and Japan's third-quarter growth figures on Sunday evening (US time).

items.headline: ECB set for last rate hike in December but inflation risks keep door open for one more: Reuters poll
items.story_title: European Central Bank: one more rate rise, then a pause?
items.summary: All 71 economists in a Reuters survey expect the European Central Bank to raise its deposit rate to 2.75% in December, but about two-thirds think that will be the last rise, fewer than markets expect.

beats.was: The European Central Bank has raised its deposit rate twice this year, in June and September, to 2.5%, because euro-area inflation climbed to 4% in October, about double its 2% goal. Markets expect two or three more rises by the end of next year.
beats.happened: In a Reuters survey taken November 10 to 12, every one of 71 economists expects a quarter-point rise to 2.75% in December. 46 of them see that as the peak; 25 expect one more, most likely early next year. They also nudged up their forecasts for inflation and growth.
beats.means: A December rise looks settled. The open question is what comes after, and most economists think the bank stops sooner than markets are betting. Cheaper oil helps, but low gas stocks before winter could push prices up again.
beats.fx: Little news for the euro on December itself; if the bank signals a pause after that, it would take away some support the euro gets from expected rises.

impact.why: A December rise is expected by all, but most economists see it as the last, fewer than markets price.

items.watch: European Central Bank speakers on what follows December, and euro-area inflation for November; a cold winter that lifts gas prices would revive the case for more rises.

items.headline: Sterling steady after UK GDP data; Fed official up next
items.story_title: Bank of England: rates rise again to fight energy costs
items.summary: Britain's economy grew 0.7% in the third quarter, its fastest in about two and a half years and in line with forecasts, backing last week's Bank of England rate rise; the pound held near $1.33.

beats.was: The Bank of England raised its rate to 4% last Thursday, its first rise in more than three years, to stop high energy costs spreading into other prices. Markets wanted to see whether the economy was strong enough to take it.
beats.happened: UK output grew 0.7% from July to September, matching forecasts and the quickest pace in about two and a half years. The pound barely moved, slipping slightly to about $1.327, and stayed close to its strongest against the euro since May 2025.
beats.means: Solid growth makes it easier for the Bank of England to raise rates again; markets put roughly a 75% chance on another rise in December. Because the figure matched forecasts, it confirms the story rather than changing it.
beats.fx: A mild support for the pound, especially against the euro; against the dollar, US rate talk matters more for now.

impact.why: Growth in line with forecasts backs the case for another Bank of England rise.

items.watch: Bank of England speakers on December, and UK inflation figures next week; weak price data would cool the case for a second rise.

items.headline: Energy dented by reports that Vance and Rezaei could meet, Dutch TTF outperforms
items.story_title: US–Iran talks: Hormuz reopening offer vs ship attacks
items.summary: Oil slipped back below $92 a barrel on a Wall Street Journal report that US Vice President JD Vance could meet Iran's security chief Mohsen Rezaei, even as Iran's Revolutionary Guards reported two more tanker blasts near the Strait of Hormuz.

beats.was: Since the US–Iran war began, ships near the Strait of Hormuz, the route for about a fifth of the world's oil, have been hit again and again, keeping Brent crude above $90. Tehran has publicly denied holding talks with Washington.
beats.happened: Iran's Revolutionary Guards said two oil-carrying ships were hit by explosions in the strait, briefly lifting Brent to about $93.90. Prices then fell back to just under $92 after the Wall Street Journal reported that Vance might meet Rezaei directly. Neither side has confirmed a meeting.
beats.means: The chance of direct high-level talks is the clearest sign yet that diplomacy could ease the supply threat, but ships are still being attacked, so the risk to oil flows remains.
beats.fx: Softer oil weighs a little on the Canadian dollar and helps oil importers such as Japan and the euro area; a confirmed meeting would push further that way.

impact.why: Talk of direct US–Iran contact pulls prices down while new ship blasts keep the risk alive.
Canada's main export swings with the odds of a Gulf deal.

items.watch: Whether Washington or Tehran confirms a Vance–Rezaei meeting, and any new attacks on ships near Hormuz.

items.headline: Nvidia shares fall on reports board may oust CEO Jensen Huang
items.story_title: Nvidia: chief executive Jensen Huang steps down
items.summary: Nvidia shares dropped more than 8% after US hours on reports that its board met to decide whether to remove chief executive Jensen Huang, dragging Asian tech stocks and US futures lower.

beats.was: Nvidia, the chipmaker at the heart of the AI boom and one of the world's biggest companies, opened an independent probe on Sunday after reports that Jensen Huang, its co-founder and chief executive, had an affair with a woman suspected of spying for China. The board said then that it still backed him.
beats.happened: The Wall Street Journal reported late Wednesday that the board was preparing to push Huang out, and Reuters said the board met that night to decide. The shares fell more than 8% in after-hours trading, Taiwan's stock market lost 2.6% and US Nasdaq futures slipped; Nvidia has not commented.
beats.means: Losing the founder who built the company would shake confidence in the AI trade that has carried global stocks. So far the hit is mostly to tech shares, with no wider rush out of risk; currencies have barely moved.
beats.fx: A mild push toward safe havens like the yen and Swiss franc and away from risk-linked currencies like the Australian dollar, if the selling spreads beyond tech.

impact.why: A tech-led stock slide can bring some safe-haven buying, though the yen barely moved.
Falling Asian tech shares weigh on risk-linked currencies.
Mild safe-haven pull if stocks keep falling.

items.watch: Whether Nvidia's board confirms a change at the top, and whether the selling spreads from tech into wider stock markets when New York opens.

items.headline: Oil prices drop more than $1 as hopes for Iran, Ukraine peace talks pressure markets
items.story_title: US–Iran talks: Hormuz reopening offer vs ship attacks
items.summary: Brent crude fell about 1% to near $91.60 a barrel in Asian trade as hopes grew for peace talks on both Iran and Ukraine, giving back Wednesday's rise.

beats.was: Oil has swung with the US–Iran war: tankers near the Strait of Hormuz, the route for about a fifth of the world's oil, keep being hit, while talks to reopen it come and go. Brent rose about 1.4% on Wednesday after a two-month low the day before.
beats.happened: Brent dropped about $1.14 to roughly $91.60 and US crude to about $85.50. Traders pointed to quiet efforts toward a Russia–Ukraine ceasefire after Abu Dhabi talks ended with a prisoner swap, and to lower odds of a bigger Iran clash before next week's US–China summit. Higher OPEC+ output in October and a large rise in US crude stocks added to the fall.
beats.means: With supply rising and diplomacy alive on two fronts, the war premium in oil is fading, though ongoing attacks on tankers stop prices falling much further.
beats.fx: Cheaper oil weighs a little on the Canadian dollar and eases price pressure for oil importers like Japan and the euro area.

impact.why: Peace hopes and more supply chip away at the war premium.
Canada's main export is worth a little less.

items.watch: Official US crude stock figures due Thursday after a one-day delay, and any reply from Washington to Iran's Hormuz plan; a fresh tanker attack would lift prices again.

items.headline: Deutsche Bank sees 3 straight Fed hikes after hot CPI, adding a January move
items.story_title: Fed: how fast to raise rates after hot inflation
items.summary: Deutsche Bank now expects the Federal Reserve to raise rates in December, January and March, adding a January rise after Tuesday's hot US inflation figures.

beats.was: The Federal Reserve's rate sits at 3.75–4%. US consumer prices rose 0.4% in October, more than the 0.3% expected, and some Fed officials have since argued for bigger or faster rises.
beats.happened: Deutsche Bank changed its forecast to three quarter-point rises in a row, in December, January and March, which would take the rate to 4.50–4.75%; before, it saw a pause in January. It does not expect a half-point rise in December but won't rule it out. UBS still sees two rises, in December and March.
beats.means: Big banks are lining up behind a longer run of US rate rises, not just one. Markets already price a December rise as near certain, so the new part is how many follow.
beats.fx: Supports the dollar, adding to its climb to a 19-month high; weighs on the yen and gold, which pay no or little interest by comparison.

impact.why: Another big bank expects a longer run of Fed rate rises.
Higher expected US rates make gold less attractive.

items.watch: New York Fed President John Williams speaks later Thursday and US producer prices come Friday; a soft reading would trim bets on a January rise.

items.headline: US-Iran talks stalled amid warnings of military conflict as Iran pushes 'two-day plan'
items.story_title: US–Iran: talk of a deal vs attacks on Gulf shipping
items.summary: Iran has offered, through Qatar, a two-day path to reopening the Strait of Hormuz, but says Washington has not answered, and an aide claims the US is weighing limited air strikes.

beats.was: The US–Iran war, now eight months old, has largely shut the Strait of Hormuz, the route for about a fifth of the world's oil. Iran sent the US a list of seven conditions for reopening it.
beats.happened: Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Iran's parliament speaker and its lead negotiator, said the US has not formally replied. Iran's latest offer squeezes its plan into two days: first the US lifts its blockade of Iranian ports and eases oil sanctions, then Iran reopens the strait. A Ghalibaf adviser claimed the US has given itself about two weeks before President Trump decides on new strikes, and Iran's top security official warned it would hit US bases if attacked.
beats.means: There is a deal on paper, but the two sides are still apart and the talk of strikes is getting louder. Until Washington answers, Gulf oil stays tight and the risk of a fresh flare-up stays alive.
beats.fx: Supports oil and oil exporters like the Canadian dollar; a real step toward a deal would do the opposite and help big oil importers such as Japan and the euro area.

impact.why: A clear offer to reopen the strait, but no US reply and talk of new strikes.
Canada's main export swings with the odds of a Gulf deal.

items.watch: Any formal US reply to Iran's offer through Qatar, and whether the two-week strike window an Iranian aide described is confirmed by Washington.

items.headline: Dollar advances against major peers
items.story_title: Fed: a December rate rise and what US inflation says
items.summary: The dollar ended Wednesday at its highest since April 2025 against major currencies, as big banks added more US rate rises to their forecasts.

beats.was: US consumer prices rose faster than expected in October, and Federal Reserve officials including Governor Christopher Waller and Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan have talked of bigger or more rate rises.
beats.happened: The dollar index rose about 0.6% to near 102.9. The euro fell to about $1.11, its lowest since May 2025, and the dollar reached nearly 160 yen. Goldman Sachs now expects Fed rises in December and March, and Deutsche Bank in December, January and March.
beats.means: Markets are no longer asking whether the Fed raises rates in December, but how many more follow. That gives the dollar a steady lift against currencies whose central banks are moving more slowly.
beats.fx: Broad dollar strength, felt most by the euro and the yen.

impact.why: Major banks now expect a run of Fed rises, pushing the dollar to a 19-month high.
The euro fell to its lowest since May 2025 as the rate gap with the US widens.
The dollar reached nearly 160 yen, where Japan has stepped in before.

items.watch: US producer prices on Friday and Fed speakers this week; a softer reading would slow the dollar's climb.

items.headline: Yen slides toward 160.00 with Fed speakers and US PPI ahead
items.story_title: Japan's fight to prop up the yen
items.summary: The dollar climbed to just under 160 yen, its highest since early September, as bets on a December US rate rise firmed. Japan has stepped in to buy yen near this level before.

beats.was: The dollar had spent seven weeks between about 156 and 159 yen. US rates sit at 3.75–4.00% against 1.25% in Japan, and Japan spent a record sum buying yen this summer to slow its fall.
beats.happened: After hotter-than-expected US inflation figures on Tuesday and Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller calling a December rise likely, the dollar broke out of that range and reached just under 160 yen on Wednesday.
beats.means: The wide gap between US and Japanese rates keeps pulling money out of the yen. But 160 is where Japan's Finance Ministry has acted before, and the last two times the dollar went above it, it fell more than five yen within a week.
beats.fx: Rate gaps push the yen weaker; the risk of Japanese buying, and a possible Bank of Japan rise on December 17–18, push the other way.

impact.why: The yen is at its weakest in over two months, though official buying near 160 is a real risk.
Firm bets on a December Fed rise keep the dollar in demand.

items.watch: Warnings from Japan's Finance Ministry, Japan's third-quarter growth figures on Sunday evening (US time), and US producer prices on Friday.

items.headline: AI cheer banishes rate hike fear
items.story_title: AI stocks: sell-off, then a rebound
items.summary: Stocks bounced on Wednesday as cloud-computing firm CoreWeave gave an upbeat outlook, even as the dollar hit a 19-month high and gold slipped back under $4,000.

beats.was: Shares in artificial-intelligence companies had sold off after the US midterm elections, and Tuesday's hot inflation figures added fear of faster Federal Reserve rate rises.
beats.happened: CoreWeave jumped about 20% on a strong outlook and chipmaker Nvidia recovered. The S&P 500 rose 1.3%, chip stocks 5.6%, and Europe's main index closed at a record. Gold fell about 1% to below $4,000 an ounce.
beats.means: Investors are willing to buy shares again despite the prospect of higher US rates, which calms nerves for now. A Reuters columnist notes that mixed messages from Fed officials are adding to the confusion.
beats.fx: Calmer markets reduce demand for safe havens like the yen and Swiss franc, and support riskier currencies such as the Australian dollar.

impact.why: Gold slipped back under $4,000 as higher US rates and calmer stocks cut its appeal.
A rally in shares lowers demand for the yen as a safe place to park money.
Rising stocks help currencies tied to global growth.

items.watch: UK growth figures and a US 30-year bond sale on Thursday; another slide in AI shares would undo the calm.

items.headline: As higher prices spread through the US economy, Fed officials weigh faster rate rises
items.story_title: Fed: how fast to raise rates after hot inflation
items.summary: With US inflation back up to 4% a year, several Federal Reserve officials now say price rises are spreading beyond energy, and markets see a December rate rise as almost certain.

beats.was: The Federal Reserve raised its key rate in September to fight inflation pushed up by the Iran war's oil shock, then held it near 3.9% in late October.
beats.happened: October figures out Tuesday showed US prices up 4% from a year earlier, from 3.7% in September, with gadgets like phones and TVs rising fast. Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan backed at least two more quarter-point rises, Governor Christopher Waller said the figures justify weighing a half-point step, and Governor Michelle Bowman said price pressure may be widening. Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson prefers slow, gradual rises, and Fed Chair Kevin Warsh declined to say what comes next.
beats.means: Markets put about a 90% chance on a rise at the December 8–9 meeting and now see better-than-even odds of another in January, a big jump in two days. The debate inside the Fed is now about pace, not direction.
beats.fx: Higher expected US rates support the dollar, especially against low-rate currencies like the yen, and weigh on gold, which pays no interest.

impact.why: More Fed officials lean toward faster rises, adding to bets already made after Tuesday's inflation figures.
A wider gap between US and Japanese rates keeps pressure on the yen.
Higher US rates make holding gold less attractive.

items.watch: Fed speakers ahead of their December 8–9 meeting, and November's US inflation figures; a softer reading or a cautious word from Chair Warsh would cool the bets.

items.headline: OPEC+ oil output climbs back close to its pre-war level in October, led by Saudi Arabia
items.story_title: US–Iran: talk of a deal vs attacks on Gulf shipping
items.summary: OPEC's monthly report shows the group and its allies pumped about 2 million barrels a day more in October than in September, with Saudi Arabia nearly back to where it was before the Iran war.

beats.was: The war with Iran cut Gulf oil supply sharply because tankers struggle to pass the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow sea lane that carries much of the world's oil.
beats.happened: OPEC's monthly report, out Wednesday, shows output by OPEC and allies such as Russia rose to about 41.2 million barrels a day in October, about 97% of February's pre-war level. Saudi Arabia told the group it pumped about 10.56 million barrels a day, up roughly a quarter from September, as Gulf producers move oil from ship to ship to get round the disruption. OPEC left its demand forecasts for 2026 and 2027 unchanged.
beats.means: Supply is coming back faster than the headlines about attacks on ships suggest, which caps how far oil can rise if shipping stays open. The group meets online on November 29 to set its 2027 output targets.
beats.fx: More supply is a mild weight on oil and on currencies tied to it, like the Canadian dollar, but for now fresh attacks on tankers are pushing oil the other way.

impact.why: Gulf output near pre-war levels means more barrels reaching the market despite the war.
More oil supply slightly weakens the outlook for Canada's main export.

items.watch: US weekly oil stock figures on Thursday, the International Energy Agency's monthly report on Friday, and the OPEC+ meeting on November 29.

items.headline: Saudi tanker reported attacked in the Strait of Hormuz, a day after another tanker was hit nearby
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: India's shipping minister says a Saudi-flagged tanker with Indian crew was in a possible attack in the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday; everyone aboard is safe.

beats.was: Talk of US–Iran peace pulled oil off its war highs last week, but ships near the Strait of Hormuz, the sea lane for much of the world's oil, have kept being hit.
beats.happened: Sarbananda Sonowal, India's shipping minister, said the Saudi-flagged tanker NCC Fajr was involved in a possible attack in the strait on Wednesday and its crew, including three Indians, are safe. He also said a large Liberian-flagged tanker was struck by a projectile in the Gulf on Tuesday, injuring four crew. Who carried out the attacks has not been confirmed.
beats.means: Attacks are now near-daily, which keeps shipping insurance and freight costs high and makes a quick return to normal flows less likely, whatever the talks produce.
beats.fx: Brent crude climbed back to about $94 a barrel; that helps oil-linked currencies like the Canadian dollar and adds a little safe-haven support for the Swiss franc.

impact.why: Repeated hits on tankers keep supply through Hormuz at risk.
Firmer oil supports Canada's main export.
Fresh attacks keep some demand for safe havens.

items.watch: Whether the attacks continue during Qatar's two-week push for US–Iran talks, and the US weekly oil stock figures on Thursday.

items.headline: Hormuz Strait will 'never return' to pre-war status, Iran's Ghalibaf says
items.story_title: US–Iran: talk of a deal vs attacks on Gulf shipping
items.summary: Iran's parliament speaker and top negotiator says the Strait of Hormuz will not go back to how it was before the war, with Iran and Oman to oversee it together.

beats.was: The US–Iran war, now eight months old, has largely shut the Strait of Hormuz, the route for about a fifth of the world's oil. Qatar is trying to restart talks.
beats.happened: Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Iran's parliament speaker, told Al Jazeera that Iran and Oman have agreed to oversee the strait. He said Iran sent seven conditions to Washington through Qatar, including lifting the US naval blockade and sanctions and freeing frozen funds, and that they must be met before talks start.
beats.means: Even if the war ends, Iran wants a lasting say over who passes through the strait, so a full return to normal oil shipping looks further off. Iran's conditions remain far from what Washington has offered.
beats.fx: A longer squeeze on Gulf oil supports oil prices and oil exporters like the Canadian dollar, and weighs on big oil importers such as Japan and the euro area.

impact.why: Iran signals tighter control of the main Gulf oil route even after a deal.
Higher oil helps Canada's main export.
Japan buys almost all its oil abroad, so dearer energy hurts it.

items.watch: Washington's reply to Iran's seven conditions; any sign of direct talks would ease the pressure on oil.

items.headline: Iran denies talks with the US and says the Strait of Hormuz stays shut until its demands are met
items.story_title: US–Iran: talk of a deal vs attacks on Gulf shipping
items.summary: Iran's security chief Mohsen Rezaei says there are no talks with the US and the Strait of Hormuz will stay closed until Washington accepts Iran's conditions, even as US leaders talk up diplomacy.

beats.was: Since the war with Iran began, shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow sea lane that carries much of the world's oil, has been badly disrupted, and Qatar has been trying to broker US–Iran talks.
beats.happened: Rezaei called reports of ongoing talks or a meeting in Qatar false and said Iran is waiting for a US reply to its conditions, which include lifting sanctions and the US naval blockade and ending fighting in Lebanon. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said the strait could reopen within two days if those demands are met. President Trump spoke of positive momentum, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the US is open to diplomacy. Iran's Revolutionary Guards said three more tankers hit mines.
beats.means: Both sides say a deal is possible, but Iran is tying the reopening of the strait to a long list of demands, so oil supply through the Gulf stays at risk for now.
beats.fx: Mild upward pressure on oil, and a small lift for oil-linked currencies like the Canadian dollar and for safe havens.

impact.why: Iran links reopening Hormuz to demands the US has not met, keeping supply at risk.
Firmer oil helps Canada's main export.
Unresolved conflict keeps some demand for safe havens.

items.watch: A US answer to Iran's conditions or a confirmed meeting in Qatar would ease supply fears; more mine strikes or attacks on tankers would add to them.

items.headline: Iran says its enriched uranium stays in the country, and oil rises toward $93
items.story_title: US–Iran: talk of a deal vs attacks on Gulf shipping
items.summary: Iran's security chief said Tehran will not let any enriched nuclear material leave the country, a clash with Washington's demand that nuclear issues be part of any first round of talks. Brent crude rose about 1.4% to near $92.80.

beats.was: The US and Israel have been at war with Iran since late February, and Iran has squeezed shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, the route for about a fifth of the world's oil. Washington says any first talks to end the war must cover Iran's nuclear programme, including its stock of enriched uranium.
beats.happened: On Wednesday the head of Iran's security service said Tehran would not allow enriched nuclear material to be taken out of the country. Brent crude rose $1.28 to about $92.77 a barrel and US crude to about $86.80 by mid-morning in Europe. An analyst at the Swiss bank UBS said fading hopes of a quick calm-down were holding prices up.
beats.means: Moving the uranium out is one of the core US conditions, so a flat refusal makes a quick deal look less likely. That keeps the risk to Gulf oil supply in prices for longer.
beats.fx: Firmer oil gives some help to the Canadian dollar and adds to the energy bill for big importers like Japan and the euro area.

impact.why: A hard line on a core US demand pushes a deal, and normal Gulf shipping, further off.
Dearer oil helps Canada's biggest export.
Japan imports nearly all its oil, so higher prices weigh on its trade balance.

items.watch: Whether the US softens or repeats its nuclear condition for talks, and whether Brent holds above $92.

items.headline: Oil climbs off a two-month low as attacks on ships near Hormuz outweigh hopes of an Iran truce
items.story_title: US–Iran: talk of a deal vs attacks on Gulf shipping
items.summary: Brent crude edged back above $92.50 a barrel as ships near the Strait of Hormuz keep getting hit, even while talk of a US–Iran truce continues.

beats.was: Brent had dropped from the mid-$90s to briefly under $90 on Tuesday, its lowest in about two months, after President Trump called the US–Iran war 'effectively over' and held off new strikes. The Strait of Hormuz, the main exit for Gulf oil, is still effectively shut.
beats.happened: Brent rose to about $92.50 and US crude to about $86.70 in Asian trading on Wednesday. Attacks on shipping are not slowing: 37 ships were hit in October, the most in any month since the war began, and 10 more so far in November. Analysts at data firm LSEG say even a signed deal would not bring back normal tanker traffic quickly, because mines must be cleared, insurers must return and shipowners must be willing to sail.
beats.means: Hopes for peace pulled oil down, but the physical problem of moving oil out of the Gulf has not changed, so the fall has stalled. A deal on paper and oil flowing again are two different things.
beats.fx: Steadier oil gives a little support to the Canadian dollar and keeps energy costs a worry for big importers like Japan.

impact.why: Ongoing ship attacks put a floor under prices after the peace-hope slide.
Firmer oil helps Canada's biggest export.
Japan buys nearly all its oil abroad, so dearer crude weighs on its trade balance.

items.watch: Whether attacks on ships near Hormuz slow, and any firm sign of US–Iran talks actually taking place.

items.headline: Dollar holds near a two-week high as markets bet the Fed will raise rates in December
items.story_title: Fed: a December rate rise and what US inflation says
items.summary: The dollar kept Tuesday's gains in Asian trading as traders now see a December Federal Reserve rate rise as near-certain and give better-than-even odds of another in January.

beats.was: US consumer prices rose faster than expected in October, and Fed officials Christopher Waller and Lorie Logan have since argued for bigger or more rate rises. The Fed's next decision is on December 9.
beats.happened: The dollar index, which tracks the dollar against six major currencies, held near 102.2, close to a two-week high. Futures pricing puts the chance of a quarter-point December rise at about 92%, up from 84% a day earlier, with the rest on a half-point move; no-change is no longer priced. Markets now see a second rise in January as more likely than not. US bond markets are shut on Wednesday for Veterans Day, with no US data due.
beats.means: Markets have moved from 'will the Fed raise rates?' to 'by how much, and how many times?' That keeps US rates high relative to most other countries.
beats.fx: Higher expected US rates support the dollar, with the yen most exposed because Japan's rates are far lower; a quiet US holiday means little to shift that today.

impact.why: Rising odds of more Fed rate rises hold the dollar near recent highs, though much is already priced.
A wider US–Japan rate gap keeps pressure on the yen near 158.7 per dollar.

items.watch: Fed speakers and US data later this week; any sign October's inflation jump was a one-off would cut the odds of a half-point rise.

items.headline: Another tanker hit in the Strait of Hormuz, this time by a mine, Iran's army says
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: Iran's army said an oil tanker struck a mine and caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz, a day after its Revolutionary Guards said three tankers were set alight there. India said a ship with Indian crew was also hit in the Gulf.

beats.was: Since the war began in late February, Iran has limited traffic through the Strait of Hormuz and says it targets ships that cross without its permission. The US military recently said all mines in the strait had been cleared, and it has been escorting tankers out.
beats.happened: On Wednesday Iran's army said a tanker hit a mine and caught fire in the strait. Separately, India's shipping minister said a Liberia-flagged tanker with Indian crew was struck by a projectile in the Gulf, injuring four. On Tuesday Iran's Revolutionary Guards said three tankers had burned. Brent crude was little changed near $91.70 at the time.
beats.means: A mine strike so soon after the US said the waters were clear suggests that reopening the route safely will take longer than hoped, whatever happens in talks.
beats.fx: Keeps a supply-risk floor under oil, a mild help for the Canadian dollar and a cost for oil importers such as Japan.

impact.why: Fresh ship damage and doubt over mine clearing keep supply risk alive.
Ongoing Gulf attacks keep some demand for safe places to park money.
Higher oil costs weigh on Japan as a big energy importer.

items.watch: How many ships are hit this month compared with October's 37, and any word from the US military on mines.

items.headline: Dollar climbs to a four-week high in London trading as bets on a bigger Fed rate rise grow
items.story_title: Fed: a December rate rise and what US inflation says
items.summary: The dollar pushed on to its strongest level in four weeks on Wednesday morning in Europe, as traders raised the odds that the Federal Reserve lifts rates by half a point in December.

beats.was: US consumer prices rose faster than expected in October, and Fed Governor Christopher Waller had said a reading like that would justify a half-point December rise instead of a quarter-point one. The Fed's next decision is on December 9.
beats.happened: The dollar index, which measures the dollar against six major currencies, rose about 0.2% to near 102.5, a four-week high. The euro slipped to about $1.114, the pound held near $1.33, the dollar reached about 158.9 yen and the Swiss franc touched a two-week low. Futures pricing put the chance of a quarter-point rise near 85%, down from about 92% overnight, with the rest on a half-point move.
beats.means: A rise in December is taken as given; the shift now is toward a bigger step, and a second rise in January is seen as more likely than not. That keeps US rates well above most others.
beats.fx: The dollar gains broadly, and the yen is closest to 160 per dollar, a level where Japan stepped in to buy yen this summer.

impact.why: Growing odds of a half-point Fed rise extend the dollar's gains after the inflation surprise.
The yen nears 160 per dollar as the US–Japan rate gap stays wide.
The franc slips to a two-week low against a firmer dollar.
The euro eases toward $1.114 as US rate expectations climb.

items.watch: US producer prices on Friday, and whether Japan's finance ministry warns about the yen as it nears 160 per dollar.

items.headline: Australian investor home lending plunges 32% in Q3 as tax curbs and RBA hikes bite harder
items.story_title: RBA: is 4.85% the peak?
items.summary: New home loans in Australia fell 15.5% in the July–September quarter, about twice the drop forecast, led by a 32% fall in loans to property investors.

beats.was: The Reserve Bank of Australia has raised its cash rate five times this year to 4.85%, the highest since 2008, and the government ended a key tax break for investors buying existing homes in its May budget. At its November meeting the bank dropped its line about more rises to come.
beats.happened: The Australian Bureau of Statistics said the value of new home loans fell 15.5% in the third quarter, against a forecast fall of about 8% and after a 5.2% fall in the second quarter. Loans to investors fell 32.3% and loans to people buying a home to live in fell 5.3%. Commonwealth Bank, the country's biggest lender, said the same morning that home loan applications were 16% lower than a year earlier.
beats.means: Higher rates and the tax change are cooling housing faster than expected, which adds to the case that the central bank has done enough and may hold from here.
beats.fx: A cooling housing market makes another Australian rate rise less likely, a mild weight on the Australian dollar, which was steady near 68.6 US cents after falling on Tuesday.

impact.why: Home lending fell twice as much as forecast, a sign rates are biting and the central bank may stop raising them.

items.watch: Australia's October jobs report on Thursday: further weakness would firm up the view that the cash rate has peaked at 4.85%.
